title: Tannaim and Amoraim: Academies, Empires and the Editors
bigQuestion: How did teachers in two lands, under two empires, turn three centuries of argument into one Talmud?

story.title: The Partner Who Argued Back
story.kicker: A great teacher gains a student who questions everything, and then loses him.
paragraphs: The Talmud tells a story set in the Land of Israel in the 200s CE. Rabbi Yochanan, a teacher in Tiberias, was bathing in the Jordan River. A strong man leaped across the water toward him. The Talmud says this man was Shimon ben Lakish, a bandit. Rabbi Yochanan looked at him and said, in effect, "Your strength should be for Torah."

Resh Lakish, as he came to be called, took up study. The Talmud says he married Rabbi Yochanan's sister. Soon he became a great scholar himself. The two studied as partners. Whenever Rabbi Yochanan taught a point, Resh Lakish raised objection after objection. Rabbi Yochanan answered each one, and the law grew clear between them.

One day they argued about a small question of law. Words grew sharp. Rabbi Yochanan hinted at Resh Lakish's old life as a bandit. Resh Lakish was deeply hurt. The Talmud says he fell ill and died soon after. It tells this part briefly, and many readers see in it a warning about hurtful words.

The rabbis sent a bright student to comfort Rabbi Yochanan. The student kept agreeing, and brought support for each teaching. Rabbi Yochanan grew sadder. His old partner, he said, had objected to everything, and that made him understand. The Talmud says he wandered, crying, "Where are you, son of Lakish?" The story is in Bava Metzia 84a.
story.think: Why might a teacher feel he had lost more than a friend when his argument partner died?

lessons.title: The Tannaim: Teachers of the Mishnah
lessons.mainIdea: The Tannaim were the teachers whose words are gathered in the Mishnah, up to about 220 CE.
reading: Open the Mishnah and you meet names like Hillel, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Meir. The rabbis called these teachers Tannaim. One teacher is a tanna. The word comes from an Aramaic root meaning to repeat or to teach. Students learned by repeating their teachers' words out loud.

The Tannaim lived from about the time of Hillel to about 220 CE. Their era ends with Rabbi Judah the Prince. Rabbinic tradition holds that he gathered their teachings into the Mishnah around 200 CE. Scholars group the Tannaim into generations, like a family tree of teachers and students.

Tannaim also appear in another kind of text. A baraita is a teaching from the time of the Tannaim that was left out of the Mishnah. The Gemara often quotes a baraita to prove a point or to raise an objection. So the voices of the Tannaim echo all through the Talmud.

words.d: a teacher from the time of the Mishnah, up to about 220 CE; plural Tannaim
the first written collection of rabbinic teaching, edited c. 200 CE
a teaching from the time of the Tannaim that is not in the Mishnah; the Gemara often quotes one

look.title: A Teacher and a Repeater
look.text: Picture a study hall about 1,800 years ago. Few people own books. A student stands and recites a teaching word for word, as he heard it from his teacher. The others listen and repeat it until they know it by heart.
look.prompt: Why might teachers who trusted memory more than books care so much about exact words?

check.q: What does the word tanna come from?
choices: An Aramaic root meaning to repeat or to teach
check.why: Tanna comes from Aramaic for repeating or teaching, because students learned by repeating teachings aloud.

check.q: Whom does rabbinic tradition credit with gathering the Mishnah?
check.why: Tradition holds that Rabbi Judah the Prince edited the Mishnah c. 200 CE. Rav Ashi comes much later, with the Gemara.

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: A teaching from the Tannaim that was left out of the Mishnah
A chapter of the Jerusalem Talmud
check.why: A baraita is an "outside" teaching of the Tannaim. The Gemara quotes it as proof or objection.

lessons.title: The Amoraim: Teachers of the Gemara
lessons.mainIdea: The Amoraim were the teachers who discussed the Mishnah from about 220 to 500 CE, and their talk became the Gemara.
reading: After the Mishnah was finished, teachers kept studying it. They asked what each line meant and why. The rabbis called these teachers Amoraim. One is an amora, from an Aramaic word meaning to say or to speak. Their discussions became the Gemara.

Amoraim worked in two lands. Some taught in the Land of Israel, mostly in the Galilee. Others taught in Babylonia, the land of today's Iraq. Scholars often count about five generations of Amoraim in the Land of Israel and about seven or eight in Babylonia.

An amora treated the Mishnah with great respect. He did not usually overrule a tanna. Instead he explained, compared and asked questions. When an amora seemed to disagree with a tanna, the Gemara would ask how he could do so. That habit of careful questioning shapes every page.

words.d: a teacher of the Gemara era, c. 220–500 CE; plural Amoraim
the discussion of the Mishnah by the Amoraim, mostly in Aramaic
a group of teachers who lived and taught at about the same time

look.title: The Eras of the Rabbis
look.cite: Dates as commonly given by historians, following the letter of Rav Sherira Gaon (987 CE); scholars differ on some
look.prompt: About how many years did the Amoraim teach in Babylonia? Why do these dates all carry a "c."?

check.q: What does the word amora mean?
check.why: Amora comes from an Aramaic word for saying. Tanna, not amora, is linked to repeating.

check.q: In which two lands did the Amoraim teach?
choices: The Land of Israel and Babylonia
check.why: Amoraim taught in the Galilee and in Babylonia, today's Iraq. Their work became two Talmuds.

check.q: How did an amora usually treat a teaching of a tanna?
choices: He replaced it with a new law
He explained and questioned it but rarely overruled it
He voted it down by majority
check.why: The Amoraim honored the Tannaim's words. The Gemara asks sharply when an amora seems to disagree with one.

lessons.title: Who Is Speaking?
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara names its speakers, so a reader can tell a tanna from an amora and one generation from the next.
reading: Read a line of Gemara and you meet a chain of names. "Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav." That line tells you two things. Rav Yehudah is speaking, and he is passing on a teaching of his teacher Rav. The Talmud cares who said what.

Titles help too. A sage from the Land of Israel is often called Rabbi. A sage from Babylonia is often called Rav. Rabbi Yochanan taught in Tiberias. Rav Ashi taught in Sura. The title can hint at where a teacher lived.

Why keep all these names? The rabbis taught that repeating a saying in its speaker's name matters. Pirkei Avot praises the one who does so. Names also let a reader weigh a teaching. A later teacher may know an earlier one's reasoning and build on it.

words.d: one unit of discussion in the Gemara, on one question
a phrase that shows who first taught a saying

look.title: Saying It in the Speaker's Name
look.text: Among the things a learner does, the teaching says, is to repeat a saying in the name of the one who said it. Whoever does this, it adds, brings redemption to the world.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 6:6, paraphrased from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (1877)
look.prompt: Why might a text about study treat giving credit as so important?

check.q: In "Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav," who first taught the saying?
check.why: Rav Yehudah is passing on a teaching he learned from Rav, his teacher.

check.q: What can the title Rabbi or Rav often hint at?
choices: Whether the sage was a judge
Whether the sage lived in the Land of Israel or Babylonia
check.why: Sages of the Land of Israel are often called Rabbi and those of Babylonia Rav.

check.q: Which text praises repeating a saying in its speaker's name?
check.why: Avot 6:6 lists this among the ways of a learner, as Taylor's 1877 translation shows.

lessons.title: Tiberias and Caesarea
lessons.mainIdea: In the Land of Israel, the great schools of the Amoraim stood in cities like Tiberias and Caesarea.
reading: Tiberias sits on the shore of the Sea of Galilee. In the 200s CE it became the leading center of Jewish learning in the Land of Israel. Rabbi Yochanan taught there for many years. He died c. 279 CE, and the Gemara quotes him again and again.

Caesarea was a Roman port city on the Mediterranean coast. It was the seat of the Roman governor. Jews, Christians and pagans all lived there. Rabbi Abbahu taught in Caesarea, and the Talmud tells of his dealings with Roman officials.

The discussions in these schools became the Jerusalem Talmud. The name is a bit misleading. Jews were mostly barred from Jerusalem at this time. The work was made in the Galilee and nearby cities. Historians date its closing to c. 400 CE.

words.d: a school where rabbis and students studied together; in Aramaic, yeshivah or metivta
the Talmud made in the Land of Israel, c. 400 CE; also called the Yerushalmi
a city on the Sea of Galilee, a leading center of Jewish learning

look.title: Two Cities, One Map
look.text: Tiberias: a town by a lake, full of study houses, far from the Roman capital of the province. Caesarea: a busy port with a theater, ships from across the sea and the Roman governor's palace.
look.prompt: How might studying in each city shape the questions a rabbi faced?

check.q: Which rabbi taught for many years in Tiberias?
check.why: Rabbi Yochanan led the school in Tiberias and died c. 279 CE. Rav Ashi, Rava and Shmuel taught in Babylonia.

check.q: Where was the Jerusalem Talmud mostly made?
choices: In the Galilee and nearby cities
check.why: Despite its name, the Jerusalem Talmud came from the Galilee and cities like Caesarea.

check.q: When do historians date the closing of the Jerusalem Talmud?
check.why: The Jerusalem Talmud closed c. 400 CE, about a century before the Babylonian Talmud.

lessons.title: Sura, Nehardea and Pumbedita
lessons.mainIdea: In Babylonia, the academies of Nehardea, Sura and Pumbedita shaped the Babylonian Talmud.
reading: Babylonia had a large Jewish community for centuries before the Talmud. In the early 200s CE its learning grew fast. Tradition says Rav returned from studying with Rabbi Judah the Prince and founded an academy at Sura. His colleague Shmuel led the school at Nehardea.

In 259 CE an army from Palmyra, a desert kingdom, destroyed Nehardea. Many of its scholars moved to Pumbedita. Rav Yehudah, a student of both Rav and Shmuel, built the school there. Sura and Pumbedita stayed the two great academies for hundreds of years.

Life in these schools followed the farm year. Twice a year, in the months of Adar and Elul, students gathered for a study month called a kallah. Many were farmers and workers who studied at home the rest of the year. Then they came to learn one tractate together.

words.d: a Babylonian city whose academy, tradition says, Rav founded c. 219 CE
a Babylonian city whose academy grew after Nehardea fell in 259 CE
a month of group study held in Adar and Elul in the Babylonian academies

look.title: The Babylonian Academies, Moment by Moment
look.cite: Dates as given by the letter of Rav Sherira Gaon (987 CE) and commonly repeated by historians
look.prompt: How many years passed from Rav's return to Ravina's death? What does that tell you about how long the Gemara took?

check.q: Which teacher, tradition says, founded the academy at Sura?
check.why: Tradition holds Rav founded Sura c. 219 CE. Shmuel led Nehardea, and Rabbi Yochanan taught in Tiberias.

check.q: What happened to Nehardea in 259 CE?
choices: It became the seat of the Exilarch's palace
An army from Palmyra destroyed it
It was flooded by the Nile
check.why: After Palmyra's army destroyed Nehardea, many scholars moved to Pumbedita.

check.q: What was a kallah month?
choices: A month of group study held twice a year
A court session to crown a king
check.why: In Adar and Elul, students gathered at the academies to study one tractate together.

lessons.title: Two Talmuds
lessons.mainIdea: The Babylonian Talmud is longer and more widely studied than the Jerusalem Talmud, and both are Mishnah plus Gemara.
reading: Each land made its own Talmud. Each one sets its Gemara around the same Mishnah. The Jerusalem Talmud closed c. 400 CE, in a time of hardship under Rome. Scholars often describe it as shorter and less polished.

The Babylonian Talmud had about another century to grow. It is much longer. It is mostly in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic, with Hebrew for the Mishnah and older teachings. Over time it became the Talmud most Jews studied. When people say "the Talmud" today, they usually mean this one.

The two works know each other. Scholars traveled between the lands, and the Babylonian Talmud often reports what "they say in the West," meaning the Land of Israel. Readers today, in yeshivas and universities alike, compare the two to see how a teaching changed as it moved.

words.d: the Talmud made in Babylonia, closed c. 500–600 CE; also called the Bavli
a language related to Hebrew, spoken by Jews in both lands; the main language of the Gemara

look.title: One Mishnah, Two Gemaras
look.text: Imagine one line of Mishnah copied into two notebooks. In the first, a few short comments follow. In the second, pages of questions, stories and answers follow the same line.
look.prompt: If you found a teaching in both notebooks, how could the differences help you learn about the teachers who wrote them?

check.q: Which Talmud is longer and more widely studied?
check.why: The Babylonian Talmud is longer and became the main one studied.

check.q: What is a Talmud made of?
check.why: Each Talmud sets its Gemara around the Mishnah.

check.q: In the Babylonian Talmud, what does "the West" usually mean?
check.why: From Babylonia, the Land of Israel lay to the west, so the Gemara calls it the West.

lessons.title: Rav and Shmuel
lessons.mainIdea: Rav and Shmuel, the first great Babylonian Amoraim, argued often, and later rulers of law followed each in his own field.
reading: Rav and Shmuel lived in the early 200s CE. They are one of the Talmud's famous pairs. Page after page begins, "Rav said this, and Shmuel said that." Rav had studied in the Land of Israel. Shmuel was known as a doctor and a student of the stars.

The Gemara gives a rule for their arguments. In matters of what is forbidden or allowed, the law follows Rav. In matters of money and property, it follows Shmuel. Each is trusted where his strength lies.

Shmuel also taught a famous principle: "the law of the kingdom is the law." It means Jews must follow a fair law of the government where they live, such as its taxes. Jewish legal writers have debated its limits ever since, and it still comes up in discussions of Jewish life in modern countries.

words.d: Jewish law as the rabbis develop it
Aramaic for "the law of the kingdom is the law"; Shmuel's teaching on obeying a government's fair laws

look.title: The Law of the Kingdom
look.text: Shmuel said that the law of the government is binding law. The Gemara uses his rule to discuss matters such as taxes and customs duties.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Kamma 113a (also Nedarim 28a), paraphrased from the Aramaic; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: Why might a community living under a foreign king need a rule like this? What limits might readers set on it?

check.q: Where does the law follow Shmuel, according to the Gemara?
choices: In matters of money and property
check.why: The Gemara (Bekhorot 49b) says the law follows Rav in what is forbidden and Shmuel in money matters.

check.q: What does "dina de-malkhuta dina" mean?
choices: These and those are words of God
The law of the kingdom is the law
check.why: Shmuel's principle says a government's fair laws are binding.

check.q: Which of the pair was known as a doctor and student of the stars?
check.why: The Talmud describes Shmuel's skill in medicine and astronomy.

lessons.title: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud tells of study partners so close that one could not learn without the other's objections.
reading: Rabbi Yochanan led the school in Tiberias. Shimon ben Lakish, called Resh Lakish, had lived a very different life. The Talmud says he was once a bandit. It tells how Rabbi Yochanan saw his strength and urged him to use it for Torah. Resh Lakish became a great scholar.

The two studied as partners. The Talmud says Resh Lakish would raise objection after objection to each point. Rabbi Yochanan answered each one. Through that back-and-forth, the law became clear. This is chavruta, learning in pairs.

The story ends sadly. After a sharp quarrel, Resh Lakish fell ill and died. A new student only agreed with Rabbi Yochanan. The Talmud says Rabbi Yochanan cried out for his old partner, whose questions had made him understand. Readers take from it that a good argument partner is a gift.

words.d: learning in pairs, where partners question each other; from the Aramaic for friendship
a challenge to a teaching, which the other side must answer

look.title: Where Are You, Son of Lakish?
look.text: After Resh Lakish died, a student tried to comfort Rabbi Yochanan by bringing support for his teachings. Rabbi Yochanan said his old partner had raised many objections to every teaching, and answering them made the law clear. He grieved, calling for Resh Lakish.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 84a, paraphrased from the Aramaic; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: Why would a teacher prefer a partner who objects over one who agrees?

check.q: What does the Talmud say Resh Lakish did before he became a scholar?
choices: He was a priest in the Temple
check.why: Bava Metzia 84a tells that Resh Lakish had been a bandit before he turned to study.

check.q: What is chavruta?
choices: Learning in pairs, with partners questioning each other
check.why: Chavruta is paired study, as Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish practiced.

check.q: Why did Rabbi Yochanan miss Resh Lakish, in the story?
choices: He had paid for the school
His objections had helped make the law clear
check.why: In Bava Metzia 84a, Rabbi Yochanan says his partner's many objections made him understand.

lessons.title: Abaye and Rava
lessons.mainIdea: Abaye and Rava argued across the Babylonian Talmud, and the law follows Rava in all but six cases.
reading: Abaye and Rava lived in the early 300s CE. They studied together as young men. Abaye later headed the academy at Pumbedita. Rava taught in the town of Mechoza. Their debates fill hundreds of pages. Students often speak of "the arguments of Abaye and Rava" as the heart of the Talmud.
The Gemara gives a rule for their cases too. The law follows Rava, except in six cases. Students remember those six with a memory word, "Ya'al Kegam," made of the first letters of the cases.

The rule does not make Abaye's view useless. The Talmud keeps it in full. Students learn his reasoning, because it sharpens Rava's. Here the Gemara keeps a minority opinion in view, as it does again and again.

words.d: a Babylonian amora of the early 300s CE who headed the academy at Pumbedita
a Babylonian amora of the early 300s CE who taught in Mechoza; the law usually follows him
a view the law does not follow but the Talmud still records

look.title: Six Cases for Abaye
look.text: The Gemara states that in disputes between Abaye and Rava, the law follows Rava, except for six cases, which it lists with the memory letters Ya'al Kegam.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 22b, paraphrased from the Aramaic; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: Why would the Talmud keep Abaye's side of hundreds of arguments if the law follows Rava?

check.q: In disputes between Abaye and Rava, whom does the law usually follow?
check.why: The law follows Rava except in six cases, as Bava Metzia 22b states.

check.q: What is "Ya'al Kegam"?
choices: A memory word for the six cases that follow Abaye
check.why: Its letters stand for the six cases where the law follows Abaye.

check.q: Why does the Talmud keep Abaye's views?
choices: His reasoning is still worth learning, even where the law goes the other way
check.why: The Talmud records minority opinions because their reasoning teaches too.

lessons.title: Empires and the Exilarch
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud grew under two empires: Christian Rome in the Land of Israel and Sasanian Persia in Babylonia.
reading: In the Land of Israel, Jews lived under Rome. In the 300s CE the Roman Empire became Christian. Laws on Jews grew harsher. The office of the Jewish Patriarch, the leader recognized by Rome, ended c. 425 CE. These pressures help explain why the Jerusalem Talmud closed early.

Babylonia lay in a different empire. From 224 CE it was ruled by the Sasanian Persians. The Persian kings recognized a Jewish leader called the Exilarch. In Aramaic his title is Resh Galuta, "head of the exile." Tradition held that Exilarchs came from King David's family.

The Exilarch collected taxes, appointed judges and dealt with the king's court. The rabbis worked with him and sometimes argued with him. The Talmud even tells of Shmuel speaking with the Persian king Shapur. Jewish life under Persia had hard times too, but it often gave room to study.

words.d: the leader of Babylonian Jews recognized by the Persian kings; Resh Galuta in Aramaic
the Persian dynasty that ruled Babylonia from 224 to 651 CE
the Jewish leader in the Land of Israel recognized by Rome, an office that ended c. 425 CE

look.title: Two Rulers, Two Worlds
look.text: A student in Tiberias, c. 400 CE: the Roman Empire is now Christian, and new laws limit Jews. A student in Sura at the same time: the Persian king is far away, and the Exilarch runs the community's courts.
look.prompt: Which student do you think had more time and room to study? What in the reading supports your answer?

check.q: What does Resh Galuta mean?
check.why: Resh Galuta, the Exilarch's title, means head of the exile in Aramaic.

check.q: Which empire ruled Babylonia while the Babylonian Talmud grew?
check.why: The Sasanian dynasty ruled from 224 to 651 CE. Christian Rome ruled the Land of Israel.

check.q: Which office in the Land of Israel ended c. 425 CE?
check.why: The Patriarchate, recognized by Rome, ended c. 425 CE. The Exilarch was in Babylonia.

lessons.title: Rav Ashi, Ravina and the Savoraim
lessons.mainIdea: Tradition names Rav Ashi and Ravina as the editors of the Babylonian Talmud, and the Savoraim finished its shaping.
reading: Who put the Babylonian Talmud together? The Gemara itself gives a hint. It says Rav Ashi and Ravina are "the end of instruction." Tradition reads this to mean they closed the Talmud. Rav Ashi headed Sura and died c. 427 CE. Ravina, the last great amora, died c. 499 CE.

After them came the Savoraim, from an Aramaic word for reasoning. They worked c. 500–600 CE. They added explanations and smoothed the text. Some scholars think the opening passages of certain tractates come from them.

Modern historians see the work as the labor of many hands over many years. Many think unnamed editors shaped much of the give-and-take on each page. Traditional students and academic scholars ask different questions here. Both study the same page closely.

words.d: the rabbis after the Amoraim, c. 500–600 CE, who finished shaping the Talmud
head of the academy at Sura, died c. 427 CE; tradition names him an editor of the Talmud
the last great amora, died c. 499 CE; tradition names him with Rav Ashi as an editor

look.title: The End of Instruction
look.text: The Gemara says that Rabbi Judah the Prince and Rabbi Natan were the end of the Mishnah, and Rav Ashi and Ravina were the end of instruction.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 86a, paraphrased from the Aramaic; compare the William Davidson Talmud on Sefaria
look.prompt: The line sets two pairs side by side. What does it suggest about how the rabbis saw the Mishnah and the Talmud?

check.q: Whom does tradition name as the editors of the Babylonian Talmud?
check.why: Bava Metzia 86a calls Rav Ashi and Ravina the end of instruction.

check.q: Who were the Savoraim?
choices: Rabbis after the Amoraim who finished shaping the Talmud
check.why: The Savoraim worked c. 500–600 CE, adding explanations to the text.

check.q: How do many modern historians describe the making of the Talmud?
choices: As the work of many hands over many years
As one book written in one day
As a copy of the Jerusalem Talmud
check.why: Historians see many editors, often unnamed, shaping the Talmud over time.

lessons.title: The Geonim and the Letters
lessons.mainIdea: After the Talmud closed, the Geonim of Sura and Pumbedita taught it to Jews across the world through letters.
reading: From c. 589 CE the heads of Sura and Pumbedita took the title Gaon, meaning "pride" or "excellence." The Geonim led for over four centuries. Jews in North Africa, Spain and beyond sent them questions about the Talmud.

The Geonim wrote back. These answers are called responsa, or teshuvot. Through them the Babylonian Talmud became the guide for Jewish law far from Babylonia. That is one reason it, and not the Jerusalem Talmud, became the one most studied.

In 987 CE, Rav Sherira Gaon wrote a famous letter to the Jews of Kairouan, in North Africa. They had asked how the Mishnah and Talmud were written. His answer gives many of the dates historians still use. The era of the Geonim is often said to end with his son, Rav Hai Gaon, who died in 1038.

words.d: head of an academy at Sura or Pumbedita, c. 589–1038 CE; plural Geonim
written answers to questions of Jewish law; teshuvot in Hebrew

look.title: The Age of the Geonim
look.cite: Dates as commonly given by historians of the Geonic period
look.prompt: How long did the age of the Geonim last? Why would a letter written in 987 matter for dates centuries earlier?

check.q: What does the title Gaon mean?
check.why: Gaon means pride or excellence. Head of the exile is the Exilarch's title.

check.q: What are responsa?
choices: The first pages of each tractate
Written answers to questions of Jewish law
check.why: The Geonim sent responsa to communities that asked about the Talmud.

check.q: Why is Sherira Gaon's letter of 987 CE important?
choices: It is the first page of the Mishnah
It is the Jerusalem Talmud's final line
It gives many dates historians still use for the Talmud
check.why: Sherira answered Kairouan's question about how the Talmud was written, giving a history with dates.

review.q: Which group taught in the era of the Mishnah?
review.why: The Tannaim taught up to about 220 CE; their words make up the Mishnah.

choices: The Amoraim's discussion of the Mishnah
review.why: The Gemara is the talk of the Amoraim, c. 220–500 CE.

review.q: Which two cities held the greatest Babylonian academies for centuries?
review.why: Sura and Pumbedita led Babylonian learning; Tiberias and Caesarea were in the Land of Israel.

review.q: Which pair were study partners in Tiberias?
review.why: Bava Metzia 84a tells of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish in the Land of Israel.

review.q: Who led the Jews of Babylonia with the Persian kings' recognition?
review.why: The Exilarch, or Resh Galuta, was recognized by the Sasanian kings.

review.q: According to the Gemara, in what matters does the law follow Rav over Shmuel?
review.why: The law follows Rav in forbidden matters and Shmuel in money matters.

review.q: Which statement best matches how the Talmud treats minority opinions?
choices: It hides them in a separate book
It records them even when the law does not follow them
It follows them in every case
review.why: Abaye's views stand in full even though the law usually follows Rava.

review.q: Who ruled the Land of Israel while the Jerusalem Talmud was made?
choices: The Roman Empire, which became Christian
review.why: Christian Rome ruled the Land of Israel; Persia ruled Babylonia.
